newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament approves social security reform.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament approves social security reform.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Wednesday overwhelmingly approved three key bills that would trigger a long-delayed programme to reform the country's ailing social security system.

The bills provide for creating new pension funds and using proceeds from privatisation of state-owned firms to finance the reform. If the senate passes them before the September 21 parliamentary election, the reform will be launched in 1999.
"The social security reform envisages a much-needed overhaul of our pension system," Jerzy Hausner, a cabinet minister in charge of the reform, said during a parliamentary debate.

Without the reform, Poland's public finances could collapse after 2004, due to the ageing of the population and inefficiency of the current pay-as-you-go system, inherited from the communist era before 1989, Hausner earlier said.
Many analysts had feared that the bills, seen as a political minefield, might not pass before the election and a new government and parliament would have to start work on the reform afresh.

But the ruling coalition of ex-communists and the Peasant party joined the centre-right opposition to pass the bills, despite reservations by many pensioners -- an electorate of nine million in the country of 38 million people -- who fear the new system could lower their earnings.

The bill on the creation of new pension fund passed in a 377 to 13 vote with five abstentions. The bill on using state assets in financing the reform was approved by 375 deputies to 11 with seven abstentions while a draft law on corporate funds went through with 366 votes to 12 with 12 abstaining.
The bills provide for creation of pension funds, which would get 20 percent of the obligatory premiums now paid to the sole pension provider -- the state-run Social Security Office (ZUS).
The new funds, which people under 30 years of age would have to join obligatorily and others voluntarily, would invest in safe securities.
The government would issue bonds convertible into shares of companies undergoing privatisation and pump the proceeds into ZUS to make up for a loss of part of its premiums.
ZUS has to be subsidised by the central budget even though it gets 45 percent of all officially employed workers' wages. Subsidies to ZUS now account for 15 percent of budget spending.
Under the new system, people would continue to get a part of their pension from ZUS, which will be restructured, and get the second part of the pension from the new funds.

One of the bills also provides for creating the third source of the pension -- corporate pension funds to which employers, upon reaching a collective deal with workers, could contribute up to seven percent of the premium now compulsorily paid to the state-owned Social Security Office (ZUS).

The government estimates the social security reform would cost about one percent of Poland's gross domestic product annually for more than 20 years from the date of the reform's launch. GDP is forecast at 430 billion zlotys in 1997.
The government has earmarked shares of the best state-owned companies worth about 45 billion zlotys to finance the reform.
The companies include telecoms monopolist TPSA, copper producer KGHM, banks, power plants, national air carrier LOT and many others.
An average Polish pension is now 608 zlotys ($200), or some 60 percent of the national average wage.
